topic.description: Brazil's 2026 presidential election campaign and what it means for policy (e.g., the Amazon). Elections in other countries are NOT relevant.

news.title: U.S. halts consular services in Brazil ahead of high-stakes election
news.text: WASHINGTON/SAO PAULO — Citing security concerns, the United States suspended consular services on Friday, prompting Australia to also close its embassy two days before the country’s presidential election, fueling an already uneasy environment ahead of the high-stakes vote. Brazil’s Federal Police said on Friday afternoon they ​had carried out preventive searches in Sao Paulo and near Brasilia, but had so far found no evidence of ​a threat or identified any suspects linked to criminal organizations. The State Department did not elaborate on the ⁠security issues or link them to Sunday’s election, which has been marked by tensions over alleged foreign interference and strains between ​Washington and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s government. “We are working closely with our Brazilian counterparts to address the security concerns,” a ​department spokesperson said in an email. The department did not say when the consular services would resume. “Consular Services in the US Embassy and Consulates in Brazil will be suspended starting Friday, October 2 due to security concerns,” it said in a statement Thursday. “US citizens seeking emergency assistance during this time should ​not come to the Embassy, the Consulates, or other US diplomatic facilities.” Australia’s ambassador to Brazil, Sophie Davies, said on social media that ​the Australian embassy in Brasilia would also be closed on Friday due to security concerns, citing the alert issued by the U.S. and advising ‌Australians to ⁠avoid U.S. embassies and consulates in Brazil. Brazil’s foreign ministry declined to comment on the matter. Election tensions The State Department made the announcement at a tense moment for U.S.-Brazil relations. Brazilians will vote for president on Sunday in a race that will determine whether Latin America’s largest nation follows the conservative shift that U.S. President Donald Trump has often cheered on from Washington. Lula and his allies have warned of foreign interference ​in the election, pointing to tariffs ​and an effort by Washington to ⁠send officials to Brazil to “discuss electoral integrity.” Edinho Silva, president of Lula’s Workers’ Party, called Friday’s closures “unprecedented” in a press conference. “It makes no sense at all. It’s one of Trump’s ways of trying to ​influence Brazilian public opinion,” Silva said. Though he has publicly praised Lula’s main right-wing opponent Senator Flavio ​Bolsonaro, Trump has ⁠not formally endorsed a candidate, and the State Department has rejected claims of election meddling, but the issue has hovered over the race. Brazilian intelligence officials this month briefed a French and German delegation in Brasilia on what they described as US and Russian interference before Brazil’s election. ⁠The visit ​underlined growing concern on both sides of the Atlantic over Trump’s efforts to ​support like-minded candidates. Violent crime has also dominated the list of voter concerns in Brazilian election polls, prompting candidates to pledge tougher security measures.
news.author: Reuters

news.title: Brazil’s cliff‑hanger election could rob EU of key ally in Latin America
news.text:
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the 80 year-old president of the world’s fifth largest country, is facing a tight race in a bid for his fourth presidential term in Brazil’s general elections on Sunday (4 October). The EU, which earlier this year concluded a landmark trade deal with the Mercosur bloc, which includes Brazil, will be watching the polls closely.

He holds a narrow poll lead over Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the country’s former president Jair, who is currently serving a 22 year prison sentence for staging a coup against Lula’s newly formed government in 2023.

The left-wing leader’s third term, won by with a slim 50.9 percent majority in 2022, distinguished itself for leading anti-deforestation policies and getting the EU-Mercosur trade partnership across its long-awaited finish line, 26 years after negotiations started.

Though Brussels suspended animal product imports from Brazil on 3 September, due to insufficient guarantees of antibiotic regulation compliance, “President von der Leyen commended President Lula’s role and political leadership in the negotiations leading up to the agreement,” the EU commission said in a statement.

The Mercosur deal marked a historic diversion of EU energies South of the Rio Grande river, at a time when Europe and Latin America were both being bombarded by tariff threats from Washington.

The Bolsonaros’ professed support of US president Donald Trump have critics worrying “this election could have major implications for the direction of Brazil’s foreign policy, its global influence,” wrote Dr. Christopher Sabatini, Latin America director at the Chatham house think tank.

Election interference by the US was discussed throughout Lula’s campaign, most notably with Meta disabling his Facebook ads just days before Brazilians went to cast their votes, state-run Agência Brasil reported on 25 September.

At a time when virtually every other democracy on the South American continent has pivoted to the right, a win for a Brazilian Trump enthusiast and supporter of environmental commodification would be a setback for the EU’s climate ambitions.

“A Flávio Bolsonaro government would represent a much stronger geopolitical alignment with Washington and the Trump administration. That could affect climate cooperation, deforestation policy, critical minerals and European access to Brazilian commodities and industrial partnerships,” said Eduardo Raguse, climate co-coordinator at NGO network Friends of the Earth Latin America.

Brazil’s climate observatory recorded its biggest annual fall in emissions in 15 years, with a 16.7 percent reduction in 2024 from the previous year, largely due to a drop in forest clearance in the Brazilian Amazon, which was halved over Lula’s third term.

But Lula has been simultaneously expanding Brazil’s national petrol company’s drilling area into the Amazon’s depths.

“Lula’s government has increasingly framed critical minerals as an issue of national sovereignty and industrial policy,” Raguse told EUobserver, since the Workers' party leader has referred to Brazil’s petrol reserves as its “passport for the future.”

But along a global pivot to the right, a win for Bolsonaro’s heir or Lula’s renewed interest in fossil fuel politics would not stray too far from the EU’s current conservative climate script, and according to Socialist and Democrat MEP Leire Pajin, will mean little for EU trade.

“Whoever wins the election in Brazil, the EU-Mercosur relationship goes far beyond electoral cycles or trade,” the Spanish vice-president of the Euro-Latin American parliamentary assembly told EUobserver. “Governments may differ in priorities or pace, but the agreement transcends them.”
news.author: Gaia Neiman

news.title: Flavio Bolsonaro: In the name of the father, sons, and holy ideology
news.text:
Will “Son No. 1” become the second president from the Bolsonaro family? Flavio, the eldest of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro’s five children, is neck-and-neck in the polls with incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva as the country heads to the polls Sunday in the first round of the presidential election. 

Jair Bolsonaro is likely following his 45-year-old son’s campaign closely. For the patriarch, this is not just a matter of family pride. Sentenced to 27 years and three months in prison after his convicting for plotting a coup following his 2022 election defeat, the former president is surely rooting for his son. “Bolsonaro Junior”, the Liberal Party’s candidate, has promised to grant his dad a pardon as soon as he assumes Brazil’s highest office.

But first, the eldest son must defeat incumbent President Lula. That is not a foregone conclusion.

Brand Bolsonaro

Flavio Bolsonaro is widely considered a shadow of his father. He is not a “charismatic and popular leader", said Andreza Aruska, director of the Brazil Institute at King’s College London. “He’s not a great orator either and he can come across as lacking in self-confidence,” added Corneel Weyers, a Brazil specialist at the Paris-based Center for International Studies (CERI) at Sciences Po.

While he is running under the Bolsonaro banner, the son has also had to maintain some distance from his convicted and jailed father on the campaign trail. “Jair Bolsonaro is no longer as popular, and slightly more than half the population believes he should serve his full sentence,” noted Georg Walter Wink, a Latin America specialist at the University of Copenhagen who has studied the foundations of Brazil’s far right.

But it’s still the power of the family name that has managed to catapult Flavio Bolsonaro into a statistical dead heat with Lula in the opinion polls.

At the official launch of his campaign in July, an AI-generated video of his jailed father endorsing the son was screened on stage. The video sparked a storm, with Brazil’s Supreme Court demanding an explanation about the appearance of the AI clone of Jair Bolsonaro, who is barred from making public statements while serving his sentence. The former president had to deny authorising the use of his image and voice for the deepfake video.

Read moreBrazil's Jair Bolsonaro denies authorizing deepfake for election message

Opting for a legally risky video screening in a country where the use of deep fakes is as widespread as it is strictly regulated does not exactly signal a break with Bolsonaro senior.

Watch moreFocus: What's real and what's fake? How AI is impacting Brazil's election race

But Flavio Bolsonaro is no stranger to public scrutiny. Last month, it emerged that Candidate Bolsonaro was under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering linked to the upcoming film “Dark Horse”. He is accused of seeking funding for the biopic glorifying his father, played by Jim Caviezel, a US actor linked to far-right circles. The film was originally scheduled for a September 11 release, but it was postponed indefinitely.

Political schizophrenia

Flavio Bolsonaro actually has little choice but to campaign on the strength of his family name. “He has almost nothing else to legitimise his candidacy,” noted Aruska.

In a political environment as polarised as Brazil’s, he “cannot afford to truly distance himself from his father without the risk of losing votes among his electoral base, which would accuse him of betraying ‘Bolsonarism’”, said Chris Lyon, a Brazil specialist at the University of Birmingham.

In Brazil, it is also perfectly natural to claim affiliation with a political dynasty. “People often talk about the three ‘B’s – Bible, bullets, and beef to describe the major [conservative] political blocs,” said Wink, referring to the Christian Evangelicals, the military, and landowners. “But there is also a fourth: family,” he noted.

During his campaign, Flavio Bolsonaro engaged in a balancing act between showcasing his father’s legacy and distinguishing himself from the patriarch that smacked of political schizophrenia. While he claimed to have his father’s support and blessing, the son also “removed his name from several campaign materials in recent months", noted Weyers.

He is also “much less blunt in his manner of speaking, and unlike his father, Flavio Bolsonaro avoids any misogynistic or homophobic remarks; he is also careful not to be as aggressive towards the press", explained Wink.

There is also a shift in tone in the way he presents himself. Whereas Jair Bolsonaro “played the role of the angry outsider challenging the system, the son is more willing to don the mantle of a mainstream politician who favours compromise and knows how to build coalitions", said Lyon.

The question now is whether Flavio Bolsonaro is willing to politically “kill” his father to make Bolsonarism appear more respectable. In reality, the far-right candidate is responding to “a tactical imperative to expand his electoral base,” said Aruska. While the extreme political polarisation has certainly whittled down the ranks of undecided voters in Brazil, “there are still some left, and Flavio Bolsonaro is primarily seeking to win over a segment of women who haven’t yet made up their minds", explained Lyon. It’s no coincidence, in fact, that he often makes public appearances with his wife, Fernanda Bolsonaro.

A family affair

But the imaging upgrade is “pure media spin", according to Weyers. “We must be careful not to give in to the temptation to believe that Flavio Bolsonaro is more moderate than his father,” he said. “The ideological substance is exactly the same.”

The 2026 Flavio Bolsonaro campaign is a sort of “family joint venture to bring Bolsonarism back to power", said Aruska. Behind Flavio are his younger brothers. “There is a very clear division of labour within the clan: Carlos plays the role of the pit bull on social media; Eduardo, who has gone into exile in the US, is responsible for forging international ties with other far-right movements; and Flavio was chosen to lead the campaign because he comes across as the most diplomatic member of the family,” explained Wink.

Flavio Bolsonaro’s political career also demonstrates that he is ideologically in perfect alignment with his father. As a state senator for Rio de Janeiro since 2019, “he has championed the same values as his father — he promotes a highly repressive security policy, defends family values, advocates an economic policy inspired by the model implemented by Javier Milei in Argentina, and opposes any environmental regulations,” said Lyon.

As a Congressman, Flavio Bolsonaro was implicated in a number of scandals. He is notably accused of having close ties to the “milicias", paramilitary groups made up of former law enforcement officers. Senator Bolsonaro was also linked to a case involving the embezzlement of civil servants’ salaries, which was closed in 2025 without convictions.

The stakes for Brazil’s democracy are even higher in this presidential election, said Weyers. “The first time with Jair Bolsonaro, we wondered how seriously we should take him. This time, we know. And the fact that Flavio Bolsonaro presents a more technocratic profile makes the threat even greater.”

Lyon agreed. “His ability to negotiate and play the game of alliances could make him even more effective at advancing the Bolsonarism agenda,” he warned.

This article has been translated from the original in French.
news.summary: The first round of Brazil’s presidential election on Sunday pits two well-known names in the political ring: Lula vs. Bolsonaro. But it’s not former president Jair Bolsonaro facing off against the incumbent head of state – it’s his eldest son, Flavio Bolsonaro. He’s less charismatic than his father but just as ideologically radical as the family patriarch.
news.author: Sébastian SEIBT

news.title: Brazil is regulating AI use in elections. Here’s why it’s been a challenge.
news.text:
Dona Maria is a straight-talking, middle-aged Black woman, whose videos criticizing the policies of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva amassed millions of views on social media earlier this year.

“They line their pockets with our sweat!” she says in one clip about a supposed increase in electricity bills.

But “Dona Maria” isn’t a Brazilian voter – or even human. She’s a hyperrealistic avatar, created by artificial intelligence.

As countries around the globe are voting in increasingly AI-saturated elections, Brazil is on the front lines of trying to regulate the technology’s use in the electoral context. Its election authority, the Superior Electoral Court, passed broad rules this year, including requiring AI-generated campaign material to carry clear labels and prohibiting the use of AI to impersonate candidates.

In the United States, at least 31 states have enacted local legislation with similar rules. But globally, election regulation regarding AI has “been perceived as a back burner issue” compared with other AI threats, says J.B. Branch, director of federal AI governance and technology policy at Public Citizen, a U.S. consumer advocacy organization.

Brazil’s polarized political landscape is rife with disinformation – a challenge that can be turbocharged by AI. From deepfakes of well-known journalists to satirical videos criticizing candidates and official campaign materials, how AI use is playing out this campaign season underscores the challenges it can present to even the most proactive governments. Avatars such as Dona Maria, sometimes dubbed “synthfakes,” are part of the constantly evolving AI ecosystem here.

Not all AI use is negative, says Matheus Soares, head of content at Aláfia Lab, one of two civil society organizations running a monitoring project tracking the use of AI in the elections. But cases like Dona Maria are of particular concern and difficult to regulate. “These are very realistic characters commenting on politics,” he says. “They can have an impact on public debate, on citizens’ perceptions of a candidate, or a political topic.”

Disinformation and AI

On Oct. 4, 159 million registered voters in Brazil will choose their next president, as well as senators, federal lawmakers, state governors, and state representatives. Leading the presidential race are Lula, as the current head of state is widely known, and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, a son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Polls have the two candidates neck-and-neck.

From India to Germany to Hungary, countries around the world have been grappling with artificial intelligence’s impact on electoral processes since AI tools went mainstream over the past couple of years. It’s a particularly relevant conversation in Brazil, a hyper-online country where disinformation campaigns dominated the past two presidential elections, in 2018 and 2022.

This year, “generative AI is the big novelty,” says Diogo Rais, a professor of electoral law at the Mackenzie Presbyterian University in Sao Paulo. While AI’s uses can range from content production to research purposes, Brazil’s top electoral court is particularly concerned about its power to fuel fake news, he says.

“Brazil has a very challenging history. In 2018, we were bulldozed by disinformation,” says Camila Tsuzuki, head of research at InternetLab, a nonprofit Brazilian research center. That year, fake news discrediting candidates on the left – associating them with pedophilia or plans to indoctrinate schoolchildren with “gender ideology,” for example – flooded messaging apps such as WhatsApp. Far-right populist Jair Bolsonaro ended up winning.

Four years later, when Mr. Bolsonaro lost his reelection bid to Lula, disinformation about the integrity of the electoral process culminated in the Jan. 8, 2023, attacks on government institutions in the capital, Brasília. Many of the Bolsonaro supporters who stormed the capital said they believed the election had been rigged, repeating unfounded claims of electoral fraud peddled by Mr. Bolsonaro himself. The former president is now serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for his role in plotting the coup attempt.

“Borderline impossible”

On the streets of Rio de Janeiro, even social-media-literate voters believe they run the risk of being deceived by AI.

“If you don’t pay attention to the detail, you’ll believe what you see,” says Ana Luiza Lelis, on her way home after a day’s work passing out leaflets for a gubernatorial candidate’s campaign.

In the run-up to this year’s campaign, the AI in Elections Observatory recorded 29 cases of AI avatars like Dona Maria, though no other synthfakes obtained her level of notoriety. An April analysis by BBC News Brasil found that Dona Maria’s online content was getting similar engagement levels to those of some national politicians.

Lula’s coalition filed a legal complaint requesting that the avatar’s profiles be taken down, on the grounds that the anonymous accounts peddled false or distorted information that could mislead voters.

“Physical characteristics create a rapport with the person receiving the information,” says Ms. Tsuzuki. “And the greater the rapport, the greater the likelihood that someone will be open to the information or the persuasion of that message.”

Rafael Satiê, a Rio de Janeiro city councilor running for federal deputy on a pro-Bolsonaro platform, says his communications team generally steers clear of generative AI. “I prefer not to use [AI], to avoid running into any issues,” says Mr. Satiê, before heading into a campaign event flanked by real-life social media influencers.

Brazil has some of the strictest rules around the use of AI in elections because of the electoral court’s power to pass regulations and resolve legal disputes, meaning it doesn’t depend on slow legislative processes, says Dr. Rais, the law professor. In the United States, bipartisan legislation to protect elections from deceptive AI has failed to make it through Congress, while in Brazil, a bill for AI regulation beyond elections remains stuck in the lower house.

But even these election rules are hard to enforce, not least because of the endless nature of online content, and the legal gray area cases like Dona Maria sometimes fall into. The character’s main TikTok and Instagram accounts were taken down by the social media platforms in May, but secondary accounts have since popped up, and some content remains available online.

“Trying to regulate individual users is borderline impossible,” says Mr. Branch.

“The big question”

Brazil’s electoral rules impose a blackout on posting and resharing AI political content in the 72 hours before the vote and the 24 hours that follow it.

But observers worry about another, less visible phenomenon: the influence of chatbots such as ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, or Google’s Gemini. A growing body of scientific research is delving into AI’s powers of persuasion, and several experiments in the United Kingdom and the United States have found that chatbots can shift people’s political views.

On this, too, Brazil has electoral laws that ban AI tools from ranking candidates or emitting opinions. But that doesn’t stop some chatbots in Brazil from doing those things, according to research carried out by InternetLab at the end of August.

How much these processes and platforms are interfering with voters’ decision-making is going to be “the big question of these elections,” says Ms. Tsuzuki.

It’s “going to be something of a stress test.”
news.summary: Brazil’s polarized political landscape is rife with disinformation – a challenge that can be turbocharged by artificial intelligence.
news.author: Constance Malleret

news.title: Donald Trump's 'Donroe Doctrine' Faces Biggest Test Yet in Brazil
news.text: Brazilians head to the polls Sunday in an election that has turned into the most consequential test yet of President Donald Trump's push to remake Latin America in his image. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, is seeking a fourth term against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after his 2022 defeat. Polls show Lula ahead in the first round and the two men statistically tied in a likely October 25 runoff. The stakes stretch well beyond Brasília. Over the past year, the Trump administration has hit Brazil with tariffs, sanctioned a Supreme Court justice, designated the country's two largest gangs as terrorist organizations and revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador in Washington. A Bolsonaro victory would hand Trump the largest prize yet in a region where right-leaning allies have been winning one election after another. "Brazil's election is hugely consequential for Trump's Latin America strategy," Benjamin Gedan, a Latin America expert at Johns Hopkins University, told Newsweek. "Trump likes to brag that his endorsement helped elect the president of Honduras, population 11 million. Brazil, population 214 million, is the real prize." The administration's approach, which many have dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine" in a nod to the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine, treats the Western Hemisphere as a U.S. sphere of influence. Its priorities include fighting cartels, curbing migration, securing critical minerals and pushing back on China's economic footprint in the region. Trump and the Bolsonaros Few foreign political families orbit Trump as closely as the Bolsonaros. Jair Bolsonaro, once called the "Trump of the Tropics," modeled his rise on Trump's bravado, questioned Brazil's electronic voting system and refused to clearly concede in 2022. Days after Lula's inauguration, his supporters stormed Brazil's Congress, Supreme Court and presidential palace in scenes that drew comparisons to the January 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol. When Brazil's Supreme Court moved to try the former president, Washington stepped in. In July 2025, Trump ordered 50 percent tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing what he called a witch hunt against Bolsonaro, and the Treasury Department sanctioned Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw the case. "I want to emphasize this, this is really unprecedented, that a U.S. government would sanction an independent Supreme Court justice in a democracy for trying someone who attempted a coup," Christopher Sabatini, a senior fellow for Latin America at Chatham House, told Newsweek. "I don't think we can emphasize that enough." Bolsonaro was convicted that September. His third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, relocated to the United States and lobbied the administration for those measures. Flávio, tapped by his jailed father as the movement's standard-bearer in December, has made his own pilgrimages, including a CPAC appearance in Texas where he pitched Brazil's mineral wealth to the American right. In May, the State Department designated the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV), Brazil's two most powerful criminal organizations, as foreign terrorist groups, a step the Bolsonaro camp had lobbied Washington to take. In July, the administration imposed a 25 percent tariff on most Brazilian imports after a Section 301 trade investigation. Brazil, for its part, denied visas that month to two senior State Department officials who planned to discuss "election integrity" in Brasília, with Lula accusing them of trying to meddle in the vote. Washington responded in August by revoking the visa of Brazil's ambassador, Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti. The timing of each step lined up closely with the Bolsonaro family's legal and political calendar. The 2025 tariffs and the sanctions on Moraes landed while the former president stood trial. The gang designations followed Flávio's CPAC speech by about two months, and the visa fight broke out just weeks before the official campaign began in mid-August. Lula's government has also pointed out that the United States runs a trade surplus with Brazil in rejecting Washington's complaints about unfair trade. A Hemisphere in Trump's Image Brazil's vote caps a cycle in which Trump-aligned candidates have gained ground across the region. Argentina's Javier Milei, El Salvador's Nayib Bukele, Ecuador's Daniel Noboa, Paraguay's Santiago Peña, Chile's José Antonio Kast and Colombia's Abelardo de la Espriella, who won a June runoff with Trump's endorsement, have all embraced Washington's agenda, and Trump has openly claimed credit for some of their wins. "That part of our hemisphere is really turning out to be very much different than it was. They've gone from being left to going right. They're all going right," Trump told reporters during a White House event on September 2. The centerpiece of that alliance is the Shield of the Americas, a security coalition Trump launched in March in Doral, Florida, to coordinate intelligence and military operations against cartels. Brazil, Mexico and Colombia were absent from the summit. Colombia has since joined, signing on when de la Espriella took office in August after years of friction between Washington and his leftist predecessor, Gustavo Petro. With Colombia on board, Brazil and Mexico, Latin America's two largest economies, are the most conspicuous absences from Trump's flagship coalition. Both are led by leftist presidents who have clashed with the White House over tariffs and sovereignty. Last month, Trump urged Shield members to formally designate 24 criminal organizations as shared terrorist threats, a list that includes Brazil's PCC and CV even though Brazil itself is not part of the group. "Trump is unwilling, or perhaps simply incapable, of getting along with progressive leaders in the region," Gedan said. That leaves a hole in the strategy, he argued, when the presidents of the region's two biggest countries "are not in the MAGA fan club." Did the Pressure Backfire? Whether Washington's heavy hand has helped or hurt Bolsonaro is one of the race's central questions, and the polling record points mostly in one direction. Lula's standing improved after Trump's 50 percent tariffs in 2025, as the president cast the fight as a defense of Brazilian sovereignty and refused to negotiate over the Bolsonaro case. Trump later rolled back tariffs on many Brazilian food products amid rising grocery prices at home. The pattern repeated this summer. Datafolha's first poll after the new 25 percent tariff in July showed Lula widening his runoff lead to 48 percent to 43 percent. Flávio, whose brother had lobbied for the 2025 measures, ended up making the case against further tariffs during a trip to Washington. The race tightened only later, once the campaign shifted to crime, the economy and a federal investigation into Lula's eldest son. "Trump's tariffs, sanctions and terror designations have been a political and electoral gift to Lula," Michael Shifter, a senior fellow at the Inter-American Dialogue, told Newsweek. "U.S. interventionism activates Brazilian national sentiments and has given Lula the sovereignty issue that has some traction even beyond his constituency on the left." Patricio Navia, a clinical professor of liberal studies at New York University, sees a smaller effect. The tariffs have weighed on Brazil's economy, which cuts against the incumbent, he noted, while Lula has spent the campaign reminding voters of Flávio's ties to Trump. "The net impact of Trump policies is probably not going to matter that much," Navia told Newsweek. If Flávio Wins A Bolsonaro presidency would move Brazil much closer to Washington, though China would set the outer limit. China is Brazil's largest trading partner and the top buyer of its soybeans, iron ore and oil, and the country's powerful agribusiness and mining sectors depend on that demand. None of the analysts who spoke with Newsweek expected Flávio to cut Brazil loose from Beijing. "Like his dad, the 'Trump of the Tropics,' Flávio would bend over backwards to demonstrate his loyalty to Trump and to Trump's global far-right alliance, including on culture-war issues," Gedan said. "But he knows where his bread is buttered." A Flávio government could deliver on minerals and trade. He has floated a free trade agreement with the United States and told the CPAC crowd in March that Brazil could help end American dependence on China for rare earths, an offer that could become his main bargaining chip for tariff relief. Ted Piccone, a nonresident senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told Newsweek that Flávio would pursue deals with the administration wherever he could, "short of crossing red lines with his 'beef, Bible, bullets' coalition." He also flagged the Amazon, warning that a Bolsonaro government could roll back Lula's anti-deforestation efforts "in favor of Trump's push for cheaper beef imports and higher production of fossil fuels." The sharpest break would likely come on security. Flávio has promised a harder line on crime, and analysts expect his government would edge toward the approaches of Bukele in El Salvador and Noboa in Ecuador. The U.S. terrorist designations of the PCC and CV give Washington a legal framework for deeper involvement. Brazil's Foreign Ministry warned lawmakers in July that the designations could expose the country to unilateral U.S. military action. Security is the one area, Shifter said, where "Washington's alignment with Bolsonaro could produce a radical shift in policy." A Flávio government "would quite definitely join the Shield of the Americas," Sabatini said, opening the door to U.S. cooperation with Brazil's armed forces against organized crime. "This is a country that until 1985 had a military government." If Lula Wins A fourth Lula term would leave Brazil as the most prominent holdout against the administration's regional realignment. "A Lula victory would not represent the US 'losing Brazil', but it would compromise any attempt to build a hemispheric bloc of like-minded governments," Gustavo Flores-Macías, dean of the University of Maryland's School of Public Policy, told Newsweek. Lula's foreign policy rests on keeping ties with Washington, Beijing, Europe and the Global South at once, he said, and another term would make it harder for the U.S. to contain Chinese influence in the hemisphere. Piccone said Lula, together with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, would lead regional efforts "to forestall or mitigate the most dangerous elements of Trump's Donroe Doctrine." Still, he cautioned that "the ongoing consolidation of right-wing governments favorable to Trump will allow him to exert considerable influence in the region, more than we have seen in decades." The relationship would start from a low point. Washington has no confirmed ambassador in Brasília, with Brazil withholding approval of Trump's nominee, Daniel Perez, and Brazil's envoy in Washington has been serving without a valid U.S. visa since August. Brazil's Congress, elected the same day as the president, could also limit Lula's room to maneuver if the opposition gains ground. Shared interests give both sides reasons to keep talking anyway. The United States runs a trade surplus with Brazil, and Washington wants access to Brazil's deposits of rare earths, graphite, nickel and niobium as it tries to reduce its reliance on Chinese supply chains. What Comes Next If no candidate wins a majority Sunday, the race moves to an October 25 runoff, and the three weeks in between will test whether the White House stays on the sidelines. Trump, who endorsed candidates in Honduras and Colombia, has been notably quiet about Brazil's race so far. "Trump's going to go hard," Sabatini said of a possible runoff. "He really, for various reasons, wants to complete a sweep of the hemisphere, if you will, of all the Trumpista candidates." The first test may come on election night. Sabatini warned that the Bolsonaro camp has borrowed heavily from Trump's playbook on contested results, and said it will be worth watching how it responds if Flávio loses. "Question the electoral process," he said, describing that playbook. "If you don't win, question it early and a lot, and if you don't win, well, then you mobilize your followers." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Sam Wilson.
news.summary: Brazilians vote Sunday in an election that could test Trump's push to reshape Latin America.
news.author: Jesus Mesa

news.title: Alternative media and Trump are influencing Brazilian voters
news.text:
Alternative media and Trump are influencing Brazilian voters

By Gwynne Dyer - “Flávio Bolsonaro is Trump’s candidate and what Trump wants is to colonize Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust,” claims the latest video released by President Luiz Inácio ‘Lula’ da Silva’s re-election campaign.

 The weird thing is about half of Brazil’s voters would be OK with Trump running the country (through Bolsonaro). However nobody in Brazil thinks that Flávio Bolsonaro is his own man.

He is the son of Jair Bolsonaro, the hard right ex-soldier and former president who tried a coup after he lost the 2022 election. It was even clumsier and more half-hearted than Trump’s brief excursion in sedition after he lost the US 2020 election – but Jair Bolsonaro went to jail for his attempt.

In a strange way, Trump even recognizes the parallel, showing special sympathy for his imprisoned fellow traveler. He claimed that the senior Bolsonaro was the victim of a “witch-hunt” by the Brazilian Supreme Court and slapped 50% tariffs on the country.

And next Sunday, Oct. 4, the junior Bolsonaro faces Lula in another presidential election.

We already know that there will be a second round of voting on Oct. 25, when the other three candidates have dropped out and it’s a straight race between Lula and Junior.

It is difficult to anticipate what that outcome will be, because the two men have been only one or two points apart (i.e. ‘within the margin of error’) in every opinion poll for months.

We know where that extraordinary stability comes from, because it is the same in the United States and in many other democracies. Most Brazilians have abandoned ‘legacy media’ and get all their information from a vast network of alternative news sites, YouTube channels, social media influencers, Facebook pages, WhatsApp groups and legions of bots.

Or rather, from two vast and mutually exclusive networks of the same approach. Whatever your opinion is now, it will likely be the same next year, because little else is getting through. Moreover, in the Brazilian case, there’s not really much to get excited about.

Inflation is low, unemployment is low, and the economy is growing faster in Brazil than in most other G20 countries. A big bank failed last year, causing a long-running corruption scandal, and the murder rate is preposterously high, but relatively speaking, Brazilians should not have much to complain about, so in the end it will probably come down to ‘sovereignty’.

Lula recently warned on ‘X’ that Flávio Bolsonaro will “hand our natural resources over to the United States…If it’s up to him, Brazil will become a colony again.”

The president portrays that as a threat, and traditionally the vast majority of Brazilians would have agreed, but both Flávio and his imprisoned father Jair would see it almost as a happy ending.

Neither of them puts it exactly like that in public, but both men see the long military dictatorship of 1964-1985 as a lost golden age. Jair served it as an active-service officer and has praised its torturers (“The dictatorship’s mistake was to torture but not kill”).

His son says “there was security, there was quality health and education, there was respect.”

Actually there was terror, lies and legalized looting, but we need not re-litigate that here. The problem is how quickly people forget, and a softer, gentler version of those brutal regimes is taking over all across Latin America.

Keiko Fujimori, the old dictator’s daughter, is the new president of Peru. The father of Chile’s new president José Antonio Kast was a Nazi who fought for Hitler, and he himself had links to the bloody dictator Pinochet. President Javier Milei of Argentina is a chainsaw-wielding ‘anarcho-capitalist paleo-libertarian’.

Abelardo de la Espriella, Colombia’s new president, restarted the war with insurgents on his first day in office. Delcy Rodriguez, once vice-president of Venezuela under Maduro, has switched to being leach president under Trump and signed over the country’s oil. There’s Daniel Noboa in Ecuador and Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, and Cuba awaits its fate at Trump’s hands.

A shady lot, you might say, and they are all selling the same deal: prosperity and security in return for obedience. That’s not a terrible deal if the autocrats keep their end of bargain, but generally they can’t or at least won’t. There will be tears before bedtime.

There are only two big hold-outs to the populist wave in Latin America. Mexico in the north seems all right for the moment, but Brazil in the south is teetering on the brink. All that really stands between it and failure is one 80-year-old man – but he is a very tough old man, and if his health holds he may be able to pull it off.
news.summary: By Gwynne Dyer - “Flávio Bolsonaro is Trump’s candidate and what Trump wants is to colonize Brazil, take our riches, steal our future and leave us in the dust,” claims the latest video released by President Luiz Inácio ‘Lula’ da Silva’s re-election campaign.
news.author: Gwynne Dyer

news.title: Brazil votes with Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro tied and a small group of undecided voters holding the key
news.text:
Brazil votes with Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro tied and a small group of undecided voters holding the key

Brazil holds the first round of its presidential election on Sunday, with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro tied in a prospective runoff and a narrow band of undecided voters, along with abstention, able to tip the result.

The latest polls show an electorate that has barely moved. Quaest's survey, published on Monday, gave Lula 39% and Bolsonaro 34% in the first round, and a 42% tie in the second, due on October 25. According to that poll, 5% of voters have yet to decide and 10% say they will vote blank, spoil their ballot or abstain. Datafolha, in last week's survey, put the undecided at 2%. The other candidates — Augusto Cury, Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema — total around 12% between them.

“The vote is already crystallised in at least 80% of the Brazilian population; the question is what the remaining 15 or 20% will do,” political scientist Leonardo Paz of the Getúlio Vargas Foundation told the newspaper El País, comparing the dynamics to US elections, where the contest is fought over specific niches of the electorate. The candidates focused their final events on the outskirts of São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais, the three states with the most voters.

In the last week, both reached out to voters wary of polarisation. “You don't need to dress in red, just think that Brazil can go further,” Lula said. “If you also want change, you don't have to like me,” Bolsonaro said. The only debate planned with both, on Thursday on TV Globo, was cancelled after both stayed away and a series of court rulings.

“I'll decide right there, in front of the ballot box,” Elza Mendes, a cleaner in Rio de Janeiro, told the same newspaper, torn between Bolsonaro's security pledges and her fear of cuts to social programmes.

Turnout will be another factor. Although voting is compulsory, abstention in the first round in 2022 reached about 21% of the electorate, the highest since 1998. Analysts warn it could be higher this year and would hurt Lula most, as his support is concentrated among lower-income groups, who abstain the most.

Besides the president, Brazilians will elect all 27 state governors, the entire Chamber of Deputies and two thirds of the Senate.
news.summary: Brazil holds the first round of its presidential election on Sunday, with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro tied in a prospective runoff and a narrow band of undecided voters, along with abstention, able to tip the result.

news.title: Trump admin shocks with 'unprecedented' move citing unspecified 'security concerns'
news.text:
The Trump administration suspended all U.S. consular services in Brazil on Friday in what one political economist feared was a ploy to “interfere in the country’s democratic elections this weekend.”

The State Department told Reuters that the suspension of all consular services across the South American nation was due to “security concerns,” but did not provide additional details, including what those concerns were or when consular services would be restored.

“Consular Services in the US Embassy and Consulates in Brazil will be suspended starting Friday, October 2 due to security concerns," the State Department said in a statement, according to Reuters. "US citizens seeking emergency assistance during this time should not come to the Embassy, the Consulates, or other US diplomatic facilities."

The timing of the move was suspect, argued David Adler, co-general coordinator of Progressive International and former advisor to Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT). Brazil’s first-round presidential election is on Sunday, pitting Flávio Bolsonaro — a far-right politician supported by President Donald Trump — against incumbent Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a progressive Workers' Party member and frequent Trump critic.

“Holy s---. In an UNPRECEDENTED move, the United States suspends ALL embassy services in all American consulates in Brazil… with no justification whatsoever,” Adler wrote in a social media post on X. “Yet another fear-stoking effort to interfere in the country’s democratic elections this weekend.”

Brazilian political commentator Julio Freiress — whose commentary was cited by the Brazilian Supreme Court earlier this year — expressed similar concerns.

“Trump has already started interfering in the Brazilian election,” Freiress wrote, according to an automatic translation by X’s Grok chatbot from its original Portuguese. “There's no reason whatsoever for the United States to suspend embassy services. There's already a whiff of interference in the air.”

news.title: US and Australia suspend diplomatic operations in Brazil before election  - Trinidad Tribune – Latest
news.text:
The United States has suspended consular services in Brazil, prompting Australia to close its embassy in the Brazilian capital, two days before Brazil’s presidential election on Sunday.

In a statement released on Thursday, the US embassy said it would suspend consular services starting on Friday and advised American citizens seeking assistance not to visit its embassy, consulates or other diplomatic facilities.

The statement cited security concerns but gave no further detail on the nature of the threat or any link to the election.

The US State Department said it was working closely with Brazilian counterparts to address the security concerns, adding that embassies and consulates routinely issue alerts about local threats and developments.

Australia’s ambassador to Brazil, Sophie Davies, said on social media that the Australian embassy would also close on Friday, citing the US alert, and advised Australians to avoid US diplomatic facilities.

Brazil’s federal police said they carried out preventive search and seizure warrants in Sao Paulo and the Federal District, the administrative region surrounding the capital, Brasilia, as part of an investigation into suspected plans that could threaten US diplomatic facilities.

Police said the operation followed cooperation with foreign intelligence agencies, but that investigators had found no evidence corroborating the initially reported threat, nor identified any suspects linked to criminal organisations.

An investigation was continuing after the seizure of communications equipment, according to the police.

The closures came two days before the Brazilian presidential election, which pits incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking re-election, against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup.

If neither candidate wins more than 50 percent of the vote on Sunday, a runoff will be held on October 25.

Edinho Silva, president of Lula’s Workers’ Party, called the closures “unprecedented”, saying: “It makes no sense at all. It’s one of Trump’s ways of trying to influence Brazilian public opinion.”

Lula’s allies have pointed to US tariffs and an effort by Washington to send officials to Brazil to “discuss electoral integrity” as evidence of foreign interference.

Brazilian intelligence officials briefed French and German delegations in Brasilia this month on what they described as US and Russian interference in the race.

US President Donald Trump has publicly praised Flavio Bolsonaro, a close ally, without formally endorsing him, saying he is “watching that election very closely”.
